Clinical Reference

Diverticulitis

On this page
Inflammation (± micro-perforation) of a colonic diverticulum — usually the sigmoid — presenting as left-lower-quadrant pain, low-grade fever, and a raised CRP; the whole management tree forks on one CT question: uncomplicated or complicated?
Sigmoid >90% (Western) CRP >170 mg/L → think complicated Hinchey III–IV = peritonitis → OR Uncomplicated: often no antibiotics ~12% present complicated Only ~4% of diverticulosis ever flares
Shared

Pathophysiology

🧬

Mechanism — the story from weak wall to peritonitis

A colonic diverticulum is not a true diverticulum — it is a pseudodiverticulum: only mucosa and submucosa herniate through the muscular wall at the four points where the vasa recta pierce the circular muscle to reach the mucosa. Those penetration points are the wall's structural weak spots. Chronically elevated intraluminal pressure pushes the lining out through them, producing diverticulosis — flask-shaped outpouchings that are present in ~60% of adults over 60 and are usually completely silent. Contrary to the old textbook "10–25%," only about 4% of people with diverticulosis ever develop diverticulitis (Shahedi 2013), so the outpouchings themselves are far more benign than their reputation.

The sigmoid colon bears the brunt because of the law of Laplace (wall tension = pressure × radius): the sigmoid has the smallest luminal radius, so for any given pressure it generates the highest wall tension and the most segmentation-driven pressure spikes. Decades of a low-fiber, low-residue diet raise those pressures further (the Painter–Burkitt hypothesis), and modern data add dysbiosis, low-grade mucosal inflammation, altered colonic motility, and visceral hypersensitivity to the picture.

Acute diverticulitis begins when a diverticulum's thin dome is injured. The old teaching blamed a fecalith obstructing the neck (like appendicitis); the modern model emphasizes erosion and micro-perforation of the mucosa with local bacterial translocation and peridiverticular inflammation. Most of the time this stays contained as a phlegmon (uncomplicated, ~80%). When the perforation is not walled off, you get the complicated spectrum: pericolic or pelvic abscess, free perforation with purulent or feculent peritonitis, fistula (most often colovesical), obstruction, or a chronic stricture.

Think of the colon wall as an old bicycle tire. Wherever a spoke-hole (the vasa recta gap) weakens it, the inner tube (mucosa) bulges out under pressure — a harmless out-pouching, until one of those bulges cracks. If the crack seals over, you get a small contained blister (uncomplicated diverticulitis); if it blows out, air and debris escape into the surrounding space (abscess or peritonitis).
Gross specimen — sigmoid colon opened to reveal multiple diverticula (out-pouchings) along the wall; the silent substrate on which diverticulitis develops.
Image: Haymanj, a retired pathologist from Melbourne, Australia. · Public domain · Wikimedia Commons
Structural weak point → pressure → herniation (diverticulosis) → microperforation → inflammation (diverticulitis), then a fork into the ~80% uncomplicated vs ~12% complicated courses.
This cascade is why the therapies look the way they do. There is no drug that "treats the diverticulum"; management targets the downstream consequences — antibiotics cover the translocated colonic flora (gram-negatives + anaerobes) when there is a true infectious/perforation component, percutaneous drainage removes a walled-off abscess the immune system can't clear, source-control surgery removes the leaking segment in peritonitis, and fiber / lifestyle change lowers the intraluminal pressures that drive recurrence. Match each intervention to the step of the cascade it interrupts.
🗂️

Classification — the language that drives disposition

Two vocabularies matter at the bedside. The clinical split is uncomplicated vs complicated. The anatomic/surgical grade is the modified Hinchey stage (originally a surgical finding, now applied to CT). WSES added a CT-based scheme that better captures the modern "distant air / abscess" reality.

The modified Hinchey stage maps directly onto disposition: 0–Ia outpatient, Ib–II admit ± drainage, III–IV to the OR.
Stage (modified Hinchey)DefinitionWSES CT equivalentDefault action
0Mild clinical diverticulitis — wall thickening / phlegmon, no abscess0Outpatient, supportive ± abx
IaConfined pericolic inflammation (phlegmon), no drainable collection1aOutpatient / brief admit
IbPericolic / mesocolic abscess1bAdmit; >4 cm → drain
IIPelvic, distant intra-abdominal or retroperitoneal abscess2a (distant abscess) / 2b (distant air)Admit + percutaneous drainage
IIIGeneralized purulent peritonitis (pus, no fecal contamination)3Resuscitate → OR (source control)
IVGeneralized feculent peritonitis (free stool spillage)4ICU + emergency laparotomy
The single most consequential word in the CT read is "free air" or "extraluminal air/fluid distant from the colon." A tiny bubble of pericolic air is common and does not by itself mean the patient needs the OR — but distant free air, a large collection, or a rising lactate with peritoneal signs moves you from the medical to the surgical algorithm. Read the CT with the surgeon.

Also on the spectrum: Diverticulosis (outpouchings, asymptomatic) · SUDD (symptomatic uncomplicated diverticular disease — chronic abdominal pain attributable to diverticula without acute inflammation) · SCAD (segmental colitis associated with diverticulosis — inflammation of the interdiverticular mucosa, an IBD-mimic) · diverticular bleeding — a separate, usually painless entity from erosion of the vasa recta, covered in the Lower GI Bleed guide.

Presentation & findings — and why

🩺

Symptoms & signs — frequency and the mechanism behind each

The classic triad is left-lower-quadrant pain, low-grade fever, and leukocytosis, but each finding is really a readout of where the inflamed sigmoid sits and what it is irritating next to it.

Finding~FrequencyWhy it happens (pathophysiology)
Abdominal pain (left-lower-quadrant predominant)~70% LLQThe sigmoid sits in the LLQ; peridiverticular inflammation irritates the adjacent parietal peritoneum → localized somatic pain. Pain overall is near-universal; several days of crescendo pain (vs the acute onset of a stone/perforation). LLQ tenderness alone carries a positive likelihood ratio ~10.
Tenderness ± localized guarding on exam~80%Parietal peritoneal irritation over the phlegmon; guarding/rebound signals the inflammation has reached the peritoneal surface.
Constipation (change in bowel habit)~50%Luminal narrowing from wall edema and spasm; diarrhea occurs in ~35% from mucosal irritation.
Leukocytosis (WBC >11)~55%Acute-phase neutrophil response — but nearly half have a normal WBC, so a normal count never rules it out. WBC >15,000 predicts progression (OR ~3.7).
Nausea / vomiting~25–40%Ileus/irritation of adjacent bowel, or true obstruction from a thickened, stenotic segment.
Low-grade fever (usually <39 °C)~30–45%Pyrogenic cytokines from the inflamed/infected focus. High fever/rigors shifts suspicion toward an abscess or bacteremia; a meaningful minority are afebrile.
Urinary symptoms (dysuria, frequency)~10–15%An inflamed sigmoid lying on the dome of the bladder causes "sympathetic" cystitis. Pneumaturia / fecaluria / recurrent polymicrobial UTI = colovesical fistula until proven otherwise.
Palpable tender mass<20%A phlegmon or abscess large enough to feel through the abdominal wall.
Diffuse peritonitis (rigid abdomen, rebound everywhere)<10%Free perforation with purulent/feculent spillage (Hinchey III–IV) — the surgical emergency end of the spectrum.
Read the patternLocalized LLQ pain + low fever + mild leukocytosis is the uncomplicated phenotype. Add rigors, a palpable mass, diffuse peritonitis, or a CRP over ~170 mg/L and you should actively look for the complicated version on CT. In Asian populations diverticulitis is frequently right-sided/cecal and mimics appendicitis — same disease, usually managed non-operatively.
🪛

Imaging findings — what CT shows and the order it appears

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis is the reference standard (sensitivity ~94–98%, specificity ~99%). It does three jobs at once: confirms the diagnosis, grades complicated vs uncomplicated, and finds the alternative diagnosis when you're wrong.

CT findingFrequency / meaningWhy it appears
Pericolic fat stranding~95–98%Inflammatory edema tracking into the mesenteric fat — the most sensitive sign; a "dirty fat" halo around the sigmoid.
Colonic wall thickening (>4 mm)very commonMural edema and inflammation of the involved segment.
Diverticula in the affected segmentexpectedThe substrate — their presence anchors the diagnosis over other causes of segmental colitis.
Pericolic abscess (contained rim-enhancing fluid)~15–20%Walled-off perforation. Size drives management (<4 cm abx; ≥4 cm drainage).
Small pericolic extraluminal air bubbles~15%Localized (covered) microperforation — not automatically surgical if contained and the patient is well.
Distant free air / free fluid<10%Free perforation into the peritoneum (Hinchey III–IV) — the finding that calls the surgeon urgently.
Colovesical fistula (air in bladder without instrumentation)uncommonChronic perforation into the bladder — pathognomonic when no recent catheter.
Contrast CT (axial) — sigmoid diverticulitis: thickened, inflamed colonic wall with surrounding pericolic fat stranding, the most sensitive CT sign.
Image: Hellerhoff · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Contrast CT (axial) — a small pericolic abscess complicating sigmoid diverticulitis (Hinchey Ib); size decides antibiotics-alone vs drainage.
Image: Hellerhoff · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Contrast CT (axial) — perforated sigmoid diverticulitis with extraluminal (free) air — the finding that calls the surgeon.
Image: Hellerhoff · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Colonoscopic view — the dark mouths are diverticular openings in the colonic wall (diverticulosis). Never scope during acute inflammation; this is the healed, post-recovery look.
Image: Jmarchn · CC BY-SA 3.0 · Wikimedia Commons
Ultrasound (graded compression, sens ~90% but operator-dependent) and MRI (sens ~94%, no radiation/contrast) are the go-to alternatives in pregnancy and in young patients where you want to avoid repeat radiation. A water-soluble contrast enema is reserved for equivocal fistula/leak questions. Never send an actively inflamed colon for colonoscopy during the acute episode — perforation risk. Scope it 6–8 weeks later once healed.
🧪

Reading the labs — what each value is telling you

LabWhat it means & why it moves
CRPThe workhorse severity marker. A level >50 mg/L (with LLQ tenderness and no vomiting) gives a positive likelihood ratio ~18 for diverticulitis; ~140 mg/L is the AGA threshold favoring antibiotics; ~150–175 mg/L discriminates complicated/severe disease (at ~170 mg/L, ~88% sensitive / ~91% specific for severe); and >200 mg/L is a strong perforation marker (low sensitivity ~28% but ~93% specific). Mean CRP is ~100 mg/L in uncomplicated vs ~256 mg/L in complicated disease. A low CRP does not fully exclude complicated disease — correlate with the CT.
WBC / neutrophilsRises with the acute-phase response, but poorly discriminates complicated from uncomplicated and is normal in up to a third of cases. Best used as one input (with guarding and CRP) in a risk model, not alone.
LactateNormal in most uncomplicated disease. A rising lactate signals tissue hypoperfusion/ischemia — the biochemical fingerprint of the septic or perforated patient heading for the ICU and the OR.
ProcalcitoninAdjunct that trends with bacterial infection severity; higher levels correlate with complicated disease/bacteremia. Not required for diagnosis; useful when the picture is ambiguous.
Basic metabolic panelScreens for dehydration/AKI from poor intake and vomiting, and provides the renal function you need to dose antibiotics (ciprofloxacin, TMP-SMX, piperacillin-tazobactam) and to decide on contrast.
UrinalysisSterile pyuria from the adjacent inflamed colon is common; fecaluria or a polymicrobial growth with gas points to a colovesical fistula. Also excludes a stone/UTI mimic.
β-hCGMandatory in any person of child-bearing potential before imaging and before fluoroquinolone/metronidazole — both to catch ectopic as a mimic and to guide safe antibiotic/imaging choice.
Blood culturesLow yield in uncomplicated disease; draw them when there are systemic signs (SIRS/sepsis, rigors) before starting antibiotics.
Histopathology — an inflamed diverticulum with peridiverticular inflammation and micro-abscess formation; the tissue correlate of "diverticulitis".
Image: CoRus13 · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Wikimedia Commons

Complications & variants

🧩

The complicated subtypes — recognize and route each

ComplicationHow it shows upManagement thread
Abscess (Hinchey Ib–II)Persistent fever/pain, leukocytosis; walled-off collection on CTIV antibiotics; ≥4 cm → percutaneous drainage; interval elective resection often considered.
Colovesical fistula (most common fistula, ~65%)Pneumaturia, fecaluria, recurrent polymicrobial UTIs; more common in men and post-hysterectomy women (uterus no longer shields the bladder)Confirm (CT with oral/rectal contrast, cystoscopy); elective resection with fistula takedown once inflammation settles.
Colovaginal fistulaFeculent or gas per vagina, typically in women with prior hysterectomyElective single-stage resection after optimization.
ObstructionAcute (edema/inflammation) or chronic (fibrotic stricture); distension, obstipation, vomitingBowel rest/decompression acutely; a chronic stricture that won't resolve → resection.
StrictureChronic narrowing; can be indistinguishable from colon cancerAlways exclude malignancy (colonoscopy/biopsy); resect if symptomatic or cancer can't be excluded.
Smoldering / chronic diverticulitisPersistent low-grade LLQ pain and inflammation between/after episodes, impaired QoLIndividualized elective sigmoid resection improves QoL (DIRECT/LASER).

Variants that look like diverticulitis (or that diverticulitis looks like)

  • SUDD (symptomatic uncomplicated diverticular disease): chronic abdominal pain attributable to diverticula without acute inflammation. This is a chronic-pain/motility problem — high-fiber diet, and mesalamine may help symptoms here (a distinct indication from preventing diverticulitis, where mesalamine failed).
  • SCAD (segmental colitis associated with diverticulosis): inflammation of the interdiverticular mucosa that mimics IBD; usually responds to fiber ± anti-inflammatories, occasionally needs resection.
  • Right-sided / cecal diverticulitis: common in East-Asian populations and younger patients; presents as RLQ pain mimicking appendicitis, is usually solitary and true (all wall layers), and is generally managed non-operatively — don't reflexively take it to the OR as an "appendicitis."
  • Pregnancy: uncommon; image with ultrasound or MRI (avoid CT). Ceftriaxone + metronidazole are generally considered acceptable; avoid fluoroquinolones and TMP-SMX (the latter especially in the first and third trimesters). Co-manage with obstetrics.
  • Elderly: atypical/muted presentation, higher comorbidity, and the greatest overlap with colon cancer — keep the malignancy question front and center.
🩺 Clinic — outpatient diagnosis, treatment & prevention of recurrence
Assess

Recognizing it in clinic

🔍

How it walks in the door

The typical outpatient is a middle-aged or older adult with 2–3 days of aching left-lower-quadrant pain, maybe a low-grade fever, some nausea, and a change in stool. They are not toxic and can talk to you in full sentences. Your job in clinic is a three-part triage: (1) is this diverticulitis or a mimic, (2) is it uncomplicated, and (3) is it safe to treat at home.

Consider instead (mimics)Discriminator
Colorectal cancerWeight loss, anemia, altered habits, older age — the reason we scope after recovery.
IBS / SUDDChronic, no fever, normal inflammatory markers, no CT inflammation.
Appendicitis (or right-sided diverticulitis)RLQ pain; imaging distinguishes — right-sided diverticulitis is common in Asian patients.
Gynecologic (ectopic, ovarian torsion/cyst, PID)β-hCG, pelvic exam/US — always in child-bearing potential.
Ischemic colitis / IBD flareBloody diarrhea, vascular risk or known IBD; endoscopy/CT pattern.
Nephrolithiasis / UTIFlank pain, hematuria; UA and non-contrast CT.
The old dogma that "young patients (<50) have more virulent disease and need earlier surgery" has been debunked. Young patients recur a bit more often simply because they live longer, but episode-for-episode their disease is not more aggressive — manage them by the same severity rules as everyone else.
Workup

What to order & when

🧪

Labs & imaging for the outpatient

CBC + CRPFirst-line. Establishes leukocytosis and the CRP severity signal (>170 mg/L pushes you toward CT/complicated). A normal WBC does not exclude it.First
BMPHydration/renal function (dosing + contrast); electrolytes if vomiting.First
Urinalysis + β-hCGExclude UTI/stone mimic; sterile pyuria is common; pregnancy test before imaging/antibiotics.First
CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrastWhen: first presentation, diagnostic uncertainty, signs of complicated disease, immunosuppression, or failure to improve. Confirms diagnosis + grades severity. ACP: reserve CT for when it will change management.Key test
US or MRIRadiation-sparing alternative — pregnancy, young patients, or when CT contrast is contraindicated.Alt
ColonoscopyNOT during the acute episode. Schedule 6–8 weeks after resolution if none in the prior year — to exclude a colorectal cancer mimicking the episode.After recovery
Many recurrent, previously-imaged, classic mild presentations in a reliable patient can be treated clinically without repeat CT (AGA/ACP). But image the first episode, anyone immunosuppressed, anyone with red-flag severity, and anyone not improving within 48–72 h — that is where CT changes what you do.
🗺️

The one fork that organizes everything

Uncomplicated disease is a mostly-outpatient, often antibiotic-free problem; complicated disease is graded by what the CT shows and escalates from IV antibiotics → drainage → surgery.
Treat

Outpatient treatment — first-line → escalation

💊

Acute uncomplicated diverticulitis at home

antibiotics are now selective
1
Supportive care ± observation without antibiotics
The paradigm shift: uncomplicated ≠ automatic antibiotics
▾
Uncomplicated diverticulitis is largely an inflammatory, self-limited process, not a bacterial abscess — so in immunocompetent patients with mild disease, antibiotics don't speed recovery or prevent complications/recurrence (AVOD, DIABOLO, DINAMO). The AGA (2015/2021) and ACP (2022) now say antibiotics can be used selectively rather than routinely.
  • Who can skip antibiotics (all of): immunocompetent; no SIRS/sepsis; able to tolerate oral intake; adequate pain control; reliable and able to return; no significant comorbidity or frailty; CT-confirmed uncomplicated disease (and lower CRP/no complicated features).
  • Supportive plan: clear liquids, advance diet as tolerated over a few days; acetaminophen for pain; avoid NSAIDs and opioids in the acute phase (perforation-risk and pressure/masking concerns); arrange a 48–72 h follow-up and a clear return-precaution ("come back for worsening pain, fever, vomiting, or inability to eat/drink").
"No antibiotics" is not "no follow-up." The safety of the observation strategy in the trials depended on close follow-up and a low threshold to re-image / admit — roughly 6–8% of outpatients fail and need escalation. Build the safety net explicitly.
2
Oral antibiotics — when the patient is higher-risk
Cover gram-negatives + anaerobes for 4–7 days
▾
When there is a genuine infectious/perforation component or the patient is higher-risk, empiric therapy targets enteric gram-negative rods and anaerobes (chiefly E. coli and Bacteroides fragilis) — the flora that translocate through the microperforation. Amoxicillin-clavulanate is the preferred first choice (ACP): single agent, covers both, and avoids fluoroquinolone harms.
RegimenStart doseFrequency / durationWhy / roleIf allergic / intolerant
Amoxicillin-clavulanate (preferred)875/125 mg POevery 12 h × 4–7 daysOne drug covers GNR + anaerobes; avoids fluoroquinolone toxicity. ACP-preferred.Penicillin allergy → moxifloxacin mono, or cipro + metronidazole
Ciprofloxacin + metronidazoleCipro 500 mg PO + metronidazole 500 mg POCipro BID + metronidazole q8h (TID) × 4–7 daysClassic combo: FQ covers GNR, metronidazole covers anaerobes.FQ intolerance → amox-clav; metronidazole intolerance → cover anaerobes another way
Levofloxacin + metronidazoleLevo 750 mg PO + metronidazole 500 mg POLevo daily + metronidazole q8h × 4–7 daysOnce-daily FQ alternative to ciprofloxacin.Same FQ cautions (tendon, QT, dysglycemia, aneurysm)
TMP-SMX + metronidazoleTMP-SMX DS 1 tab PO + metronidazole 500 mg POBoth BID/TID × 4–7 daysNon-FQ GNR option + anaerobic cover.Sulfa allergy → avoid; watch K⁺/Cr
Moxifloxacin (monotherapy)400 mg POonce daily × 4–7 daysSingle-agent option for the penicillin-allergic (has anaerobic activity).FQ-class cautions; rising resistance — check local antibiogram
Monitor when startingFluoroquinolones: tendinopathy/rupture, QT prolongation, CNS effects, dysglycemia, and aortic-aneurysm association — avoid in the elderly with vascular disease when an alternative exists. Metronidazole: metallic taste and a strict no-alcohol warning (disulfiram reaction). Amox-clav: diarrhea/C. difficile risk. Reassess in 48–72 h; if not improving, re-image.
3
Not improving / complicated → escalate care
Outpatient failure runs ~6–8%
▾

If at 48–72 h the pain, fever, or intake is not clearly better — or the repeat CT shows an abscess/air — the patient needs admission for IV antibiotics ± drainage (see Wards). Failure to advance diet, escalating pain, rigors, or any peritoneal sign is a same-day ED referral.

🥦

Preventing the next episode — what works, what doesn't

InterventionWhat to doEvidence / role
High-fiber dietTarget ~25–35 g/day once fully recovered; advance gradually (whole grains, fruit, vegetables, legumes)Lowers intraluminal pressure/segmentation; associated with fewer symptoms and recurrences. Cornerstone of prevention.
Liberalize "forbidden" foodsNuts, seeds, popcorn, corn are permittedThe Health Professionals Follow-up Study (Strate, JAMA 2008) found no increased risk — actively counsel patients to stop avoiding them.
Physical activity + weight lossRegular vigorous activity; treat obesityObesity and inactivity raise recurrence and complication risk.
Stop smokingCessation supportSmoking associates with complicated disease and perforation.
Minimize NSAIDs / opioidsAvoid chronic NSAIDs where possibleNSAIDs and opioids associate with perforation/complicated disease.
MesalamineDo NOT use to prevent recurrencePREVENT-1/PREVENT-2 negative; AGA/ACP recommend against it for prevention (it may still help SUDD symptoms — a different indication).
Rifaximin / probioticsNot routinely recommendedCyclic rifaximin + fiber has modest/uncertain benefit; probiotic evidence insufficient — not standard of care.
Prevention is like lowering the pressure in an over-inflated hose rather than patching each new bulge: fiber, activity, and weight loss reduce the colonic pressures that create diverticula and drive recurrence — there is no pill that "cures" the diverticula themselves.
Interactions

Comorbidities & drugs to avoid

🔗

How the common comorbidities change the course and the plan

ComorbidityEffect on diseaseWhat it changes in management
Immunosuppression (transplant, chemo, chronic steroids, biologics, cirrhosis, CKD, poorly controlled DM)Blunted exam & fever, atypical/quiet presentations, higher perforation and outpatient-failure rates, worse outcomesLower threshold to image, admit, give IV antibiotics, and operate; do not manage without antibiotics; strongly consider elective resection after recovery.
Chronic kidney diseaseAlters drug clearance; NSAID-avoidance already importantRenally dose ciprofloxacin, TMP-SMX, metronidazole (active-metabolite accumulation), and piperacillin-tazobactam; avoid nephrotoxins and NSAIDs.
DiabetesWorse outcomes; FQs can cause dysglycemiaInpatient glucose target 140–180 mg/dL; watch FQ-induced hypo/hyperglycemia.
CirrhosisHigher mortality; SBP can mimic; ascites complicates drainage/surgeryTreat as high-risk; caution with hepatically-metabolized drugs; involve GI/surgery early.
Anticoagulation / antiplateletsBleeding risk; and diverticular bleeding is a separate entity (painless hematochezia)Distinguish diverticulitis (pain, inflammation) from diverticular bleeding; plan periprocedural anticoagulation before drainage/surgery.
Connective-tissue disease (Ehlers-Danlos, Marfan, ADPKD)Earlier, more severe or atypical diverticular disease from wall weaknessHigher index of suspicion; individualized surgical thresholds.
Drugs to avoid / use with caution in acute diverticulitis: NSAIDs (associated with perforation and complicated disease), corticosteroids (increase perforation risk and blunt the exam and fever, masking severity), and opioids (raise intracolonic pressure and mask progression — use sparingly, prefer acetaminophen). In the immunosuppressed, the muted presentation is itself the danger — a "mild-looking" abdomen can hide a perforation.

🔗

Other tools used in diverticulitis

No single validated point-score is universally used for outpatient triage. In practice, clinicians combine the CT (Hinchey/WSES stage), the CRP (>170 mg/L flags complicated), the exam (guarding), and comorbidity. For the septic patient, the sepsis scores below carry the numbers you can verify and act on:

  • qSOFA — bedside sepsis screen (built live in the Wards → escalation tool). Open qSOFA on MDCalc.
  • SOFA — organ-dysfunction score for the ICU. Open SOFA on MDCalc.
  • WSES / Ambrosetti CT criteria — radiologic severity descriptors (abscess, distant air/fluid) rather than a bedside point score.
Prevent

USPSTF A/B & whole-patient prevention

🛡️

Grade A & B screening relevant to this patient

GradeRecommendationPopulation
AColorectal cancer screening (colonoscopy, FIT, etc.) — dovetails with the post-diverticulitis colonoscopy to exclude a cancer mimicAdults 50–75 y
BColorectal cancer screeningAdults 45–49 y
BHealthy diet / physical activity behavioral counselingAdults with cardiometabolic risk factors
ATobacco cessation — ask + counsel + pharmacotherapyAll adults
BObesity screening + intensive behavioral interventionAdults with BMI ≥30
BUnhealthy alcohol use screening + brief counselingAdults ≥18 y
The post-recovery colonoscopy and the USPSTF colorectal-cancer screening are two birds with one stone. After an episode of complicated diverticulitis the yield of finding a cancer at colonoscopy is high (~8–11%); after uncomplicated disease it's low (~0.5–2%) but still worth completing if the patient is due for screening anyway.
Escalate

When clinic isn't enough

🚑

Red flags → ED / admission

Diffuse abdominal tenderness, guarding or rebound (peritonitis) · high fever or rigors · inability to tolerate oral intake / intractable vomiting · uncontrolled pain · signs of sepsis (tachycardia, hypotension, confusion) · immunosuppression with any new abdominal pain · CT showing an abscess, distant free air, obstruction, or fistula · failure to improve after 48–72 h of outpatient therapy · unreliable follow-up / inadequate home support.
🛏️ Wards — acute inpatient management
Admit

Who gets admitted

📋

Admission criteria

Admit when the disease is complicated, the patient is systemically unwell or immunosuppressed, or the outpatient plan has failed. In practice, any one of the following is enough:

  • Complicated disease on CT — abscess, free/distant air, perforation, obstruction, or fistula (Hinchey Ib and above).
  • Systemic illness — SIRS/sepsis, high fever, rigors, or significant leukocytosis with a toxic appearance.
  • Can't tolerate oral — intractable nausea/vomiting or inability to keep down fluids/medications.
  • Uncontrolled pain requiring parenteral analgesia.
  • Immunosuppression or significant comorbidity (transplant, chemo, chronic steroids, poorly controlled DM, CKD, cirrhosis) — lower threshold.
  • Outpatient failure — no improvement after 48–72 h of oral therapy.
  • Social — unreliable follow-up, inadequate support, or extremes of frailty.
A patient can be Hinchey 0/Ia and still need admission — the decision is driven as much by physiology and PO tolerance as by the anatomic stage. Conversely, a small contained Ib abscess in a well, immunocompetent patient may occasionally be managed with close outpatient oral therapy in selected cases — decide with surgery.

Piperacillin-tazobactam3.375 g IV q6h (or 4.5 g IV q6–8h; consider extended infusion)Single-agent broad GNR (incl. Pseudomonas) + anaerobe cover — the common inpatient default for sicker patients.Penicillin anaphylaxis → aztreonam + metronidazole (+ vancomycin)

DurationFor complicated disease with adequate source control, a fixed ~4-day course is as effective as a longer symptom-guided course (STOP-IT). Without source control (abscess not drained), continue until the patient defervesces and normalizes — often a total of ~7–10 days, individualized. For simple inpatient uncomplicated disease that responds fast, a short course + transition to oral is appropriate.
3
Source control — abscess drainage
Antibiotics can't sterilize a walled-off collection
▾
  • Small abscess: IV antibiotics alone usually suffice; reassess clinically and re-image if not improving.
  • Larger abscess → CT-guided percutaneous drainage + antibiotics — removes the septic focus and often converts an emergency operation into a later elective one (or none).
  • The guidelines disagree on the exact cutoff: ASCRS 2020 drains stable patients with an abscess >3 cm (strong rec, 1B); WSES 2020 trials antibiotics alone for a <4–5 cm collection and drains those >4–5 cm. Practical synthesis: ~3–4 cm is the decision zone — below, antibiotics; above, drainage + antibiotics.
  • Not drainable / failed drainage / peritonitis: surgery (see ICU).
Transition IV → oral antibiotics when the patient is afebrile ~24 h, pain and exam improving, WBC/CRP trending down, and tolerating oral intake. Complete the (short) course orally and arrange the 6–8 week colonoscopy.
Monitor

What to trend each day

📈

Daily assessment

  • Exam: pain trajectory, tenderness, and whether guarding/peritoneal signs are receding or spreading — the single most important daily read.
  • Vitals: defervescence, resolution of tachycardia, MAP; any new hypotension = re-evaluate for progression/sepsis.
  • Labs: WBC and CRP down-trending; BMP for renal function/electrolytes; lactate if concern for progression.
  • GI function: return of appetite, flatus/stool, ability to advance diet; watch for evolving obstruction.
  • Drains (if placed): output volume/character; declining output + clinical improvement = ready to remove.
The 48–72 hour rule: most patients on appropriate therapy are clearly better by 2–3 days. Failure to improve — persistent fever, rising WBC/CRP, worsening pain — should trigger a repeat CT to look for a new or enlarging abscess, missed perforation, or obstruction that needs drainage or surgery.
Escalate

When to call the ICU / surgery

⬆️

Concrete escalation triggers

Transfer to a higher level of care / call surgery for any of:
  • Hemodynamics: SBP <90 mmHg or MAP <65 despite a 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus → vasopressor need = ICU.
  • Perfusion: lactate >2 mmol/L and rising (≥4 = overt shock); new oliguria (<0.5 mL/kg/h); mottling/cool extremities.
  • Sepsis screen: qSOFA ≥2 (RR ≥22, SBP ≤100, altered mentation) or an escalating oxygen/pressor requirement.
  • Abdomen: new diffuse peritonitis, or repeat CT showing free perforation / uncontrolled source → emergency surgery.
  • Failure of drainage: persistent sepsis after percutaneous drainage.

qSOFA — quick bedside sepsis screen (1 point each):

Respiratory rate ≥22 /min +1
Systolic BP ≤100 mmHg +1
Altered mentation (GCS <15) +1
0
Dispo

Discharge & disposition

🏠

Readiness + where they go

Discharge readiness: afebrile ~24 h · pain controlled on oral analgesia · tolerating a diet and oral antibiotics (if any) · WBC/CRP improving · any drain managed and stable · a clear plan for the 6–8 week colonoscopy and surgical follow-up if complicated.

Home

Most patients — resolved episode, independent, reliable follow-up. Diet + prevention counseling; colonoscopy scheduled.

Home health

Home with a drain in place or completing IV/OPAT antibiotics, or needing wound/ostomy nursing after surgery.

SNF

Deconditioned elderly or post-op patient who needs 24-h skilled nursing but <3 h therapy/day.

Acute rehab (IRF)

Post-operative patient who can tolerate ≥3 h therapy/day across ≥2 disciplines.

LTAC

Prolonged complex recovery — e.g., open abdomen, prolonged ventilation, or complex wound after Hartmann.

Hospice / palliative

Frail patient with recurrent complicated disease not a surgical candidate, or comfort-focused goals.
Elective sigmoid resection is now an individualized conversation, not an automatic "after 2 episodes" rule. Favor it after complicated disease, in the immunosuppressed, for smoldering/ongoing symptoms or frequent recurrences hurting quality of life (DIRECT/LASER showed QoL benefit), and for fistula/stricture. Discuss risk/benefit with colorectal surgery after full recovery.
🫀 ICU — perforated diverticulitis, sepsis & source control
Admit

ICU triggers & severity

🚨

When it belongs in the unit

The ICU presentation of diverticulitis is Hinchey III–IV — free perforation with purulent or feculent peritonitis — driving sepsis or septic shock (or a decompensating abscess). The disease is now a surgical intra-abdominal sepsis problem, managed on two clocks running in parallel: resuscitation and source control.

  • Septic shock: hypotension needing vasopressors to keep MAP ≥65 and/or lactate >2 mmol/L after adequate fluids.
  • Generalized peritonitis / free perforation on exam or CT (distant free air, large collection, feculent fluid).
  • Respiratory failure, marked metabolic acidosis, or acute kidney injury from sepsis.
  • Peri-operative management of the emergency laparotomy patient.
In septic shock from a perforated viscus, source control is time-critical — aim to achieve it (OR or drainage) as soon as the patient is resuscitated enough to tolerate it, ideally within 6–12 hours. Antibiotics and pressors are supportive; they do not fix a hole leaking stool into the peritoneum.
Monitor

Monitoring & access

🩸

Lines, labs, targets

  • Access: two large-bore IVs for resuscitation; central line if escalating/multiple pressors; arterial line for continuous BP and frequent labs/lactate.
  • Resuscitation targets (Surviving Sepsis 2021): MAP ≥65 mmHg; urine ≥0.5 mL/kg/h; lactate clearance toward normal; mentation and capillary refill.
  • Fluids: ~30 mL/kg balanced crystalloid for sepsis-induced hypoperfusion, then dynamic reassessment (avoid over-resuscitation, especially peri-op).
  • Labs: serial lactate, CBC, BMP, LFTs, coags (DIC in severe sepsis), blood cultures ×2 before antibiotics.
  • Antibiotics within 1 hour of recognizing septic shock — broad-spectrum (below).
Support

Pressors & antibiotics in septic shock

💉

Which drip, why, and the dose

Peritonitis produces vasodilatory (distributive) shock — the problem is a low systemic vascular resistance, so the primary lever is a vasoconstrictor. Restore MAP ≥65 while source control is arranged.

AgentReceptors / mechanismDoseEffectWhen to pick
Norepinephrineα1 >> β1Start 0.05 mcg/kg/min, titrate (typ. 0.05–0.5+)↑↑SVR, mild ↑COFirst-line vasopressor in septic shock (Surviving Sepsis).
VasopressinV1 (non-adrenergic vasoconstriction)0.03 U/min (fixed, add-on)↑SVR, catecholamine-sparingAdd to norepinephrine to reach MAP or reduce catecholamine dose.
Epinephrineβ1/β2/α (potent)0.01–0.5 mcg/kg/min↑CO + ↑SVRThird-line / add-on for refractory shock; expect ↑lactate.
HydrocortisoneCorticosteroid (vascular tone / cortisol)200 mg/day IV (e.g., 50 mg q6h)Restores pressor responsivenessFor shock requiring ongoing/escalating vasopressors.
Match the drug to the lesion: peritonitis-driven shock is a low-SVR state, so norepinephrine's α1 vasoconstriction is the physiologic fix; vasopressin adds a non-adrenergic squeeze; steroids are for the catecholamine-refractory patient. Inotropes are only needed if a coexisting cardiac problem limits output.

Empiric antibiotics for the septic, perforated patient

Broad-spectrum within 1 hour — piperacillin-tazobactam 3.375 g IV q6h or meropenem 1 g IV q8h (carbapenem for critically ill / ESBL risk / healthcare-associated), covering enteric GNR (incl. Pseudomonas) and anaerobes. Add empiric antifungal (echinocandin/fluconazole) when free perforation with heavy contamination plus risk factors. De-escalate on cultures and source control.

Source control

Surgery & the operative decision

⚙️

Which operation, and the trial evidence

Source control means removing the leaking segment / draining the contamination. For Hinchey III–IV the options and their evidence:

OptionWhat it isEvidence / bottom line
Primary resection + anastomosis (PRA) ± diverting loop ileostomyResect the diseased sigmoid and rejoin the bowel in the same operation, often protected by a temporary ileostomyPreferred over Hartmann in appropriately selected/stable patients: DIVERTI and the LADIES/DIVA data show similar mortality but far higher stoma-reversal rates (DIVERTI: ~96% PRA vs ~65% Hartmann reversed at 18 mo) and better long-term QoL.
Hartmann procedureResect the sigmoid, bring up an end colostomy, close the rectal stump (reversal is a second major operation)Still the right choice for the unstable / grossly contaminated / high-risk patient where an anastomosis is unsafe. Many stomas are never reversed.
Laparoscopic peritoneal lavage (Hinchey III, purulent only — never feculent)Washout + drains without resectionSCANDIV / LOLA(LADIES) / DILALA: higher reintervention rates (SCANDIV reoperation 20% vs 6%) and 4 sigmoid cancers were missed in the SCANDIV lavage arm because no specimen is resected. ASCRS recommends against it for feculent peritonitis (1A). Reserve for highly selected purulent cases at experienced centers.
Damage-control surgeryAbbreviated resection, open abdomen, planned re-lookFor the crashing patient — control the source fast, resuscitate in ICU, reconstruct later.
Feculent (Hinchey IV) peritonitis is the highest-mortality presentation and almost always means Hartmann or damage-control in an unstable patient. Purulent (Hinchey III) gives more room to consider primary anastomosis if the patient stabilizes. The stoma decision is about physiology and contamination, not dogma.
Airway

Respiratory support (peri-op sepsis)

🌬️

If sepsis/ARDS requires intubation

Diverticulitis itself is not a lung disease, but septic shock and emergency laparotomy frequently require intubation and lung-protective ventilation. Use a standard sepsis/ARDS strategy:

Mode
AC / Volume
volume-control assist-control
Tidal volume
6 mL/kg IBW
lung-protective (ARDSNet)
Plateau pressure
<30 cmH₂O
limit barotrauma
PEEP
5–10
titrate to oxygenation
FiO₂
100% → wean
SpO₂ 92–96%
Peri-intubation danger zone: induction + positive pressure can crater the BP in a septic, hypovolemic abdomen. Resuscitate first, have vasopressors at the bedside, and use a hemodynamically stable induction agent (etomidate or ketamine). A distended, high-pressure abdomen also raises intra-abdominal pressure — watch for abdominal compartment syndrome after massive resuscitation.
Downgrade

When to step down

⬇️

De-escalation to the floor

  • Hemodynamics: off vasopressors (or a single low, stable weaning dose) with MAP ≥65 for ≥6–24 h.
  • Perfusion: lactate normalized/clearing (<2 mmol/L); urine ≥0.5 mL/kg/h; warm, mentating.
  • Source: controlled — segment resected or abscess drained with declining drain output; no new collection.
  • Respiratory: extubated and stable, or on minimal support.
  • Abdomen: improving exam, resolving ileus, no ongoing surgical issue.
  • Not yet if: still pressor-dependent, undrained/uncontrolled source, rising lactate, or an open abdomen awaiting closure — premature transfer just bounces back.
ICU disposition for the patient who can't be quickly weaned: LTAC for prolonged ventilation/open-abdomen recovery, SNF/IRF for post-op reconditioning, and an honest goals-of-care conversation for the frail patient with feculent peritonitis and multiorgan failure, where mortality is high.
Shared

Pearls & pitfalls

💡

Fourteen practice-changing pearls

  1. Only ~4% of diverticulosis ever becomes diverticulitis. The textbook "10–25%" is obsolete (Shahedi 2013). The outpouchings are usually harmless.
  2. Uncomplicated diverticulitis often needs no antibiotics in immunocompetent patients (AVOD, DIABOLO, DINAMO) — WSES grades this as strong as it gets. Reserve antibiotics for the higher-risk patient.
  3. A normal WBC does not exclude diverticulitis — leukocytosis is present in only ~55%. Don't be reassured by a normal count.
  4. CRP is the workhorse biomarker. >50 mg/L supports the diagnosis; >150–175 mg/L flags complicated/severe; >200 mg/L is ~93% specific for perforation.
  5. Complicated disease usually appears at the FIRST episode, and complication risk falls — not rises — with subsequent recurrences. This is why prophylactic resection "by episode count" was abandoned.
  6. Don't resect just because it's the second episode or the patient is "young." Elective surgery is individualized to complications, smoldering symptoms, and quality of life (AGA, ASCRS).
  7. Colonoscopy yield is driven by complexity — ~0.7% cancer after uncomplicated vs ~10.8% after complicated disease. Always scope after complicated disease; after uncomplicated, defer to age-appropriate screening.
  8. Nuts, seeds, corn, and popcorn are safe. Actively counsel patients away from decades of needless avoidance (Strate 2008, JAMA).
  9. Mesalamine does not prevent recurrence (PREVENT trials) — but it may relieve symptoms in SUDD, a different indication. Don't conflate the two.
  10. Immunosuppressed patients break the rules. Blunted exam and fever, higher perforation and failure rates — image early, admit, broaden antibiotics, involve surgery, and consider elective resection.
  11. Right-sided diverticulitis is common in East-Asian and younger patients, mimics appendicitis, and is usually managed non-operatively — don't rush to appendectomy.
  12. Laparoscopic lavage is not for feculent peritonitis and carries higher reintervention rates even in purulent disease; because nothing is resected, it also missed four sigmoid cancers in SCANDIV.
  13. After adequate source control, ~4 days of antibiotics is enough (STOP-IT). Stop the reflexive 10–14 day course unless there is bacteremia or unresolved source.
  14. Primary anastomosis (± diverting ileostomy) beats Hartmann for stoma-free survival with equal mortality in selected Hinchey III/IV (DIVERTI, LADIES-DIVA HR 2.79) — the end colostomy is not automatic.
Pitfalls to avoid: (1) missing a colon cancer masquerading as diverticulitis — especially the stricturing/complicated case, so complete the colonoscopy; (2) under-imaging the immunosuppressed whose exam is falsely benign; (3) believing young patients have inherently "more virulent" disease — they don't; (4) reflexively reaching for NSAIDs, opioids, or steroids in the acute abdomen — each raises perforation risk and masks the exam.
